articles.title: What money bought
articles.content: SLEAZE, bribery, and secret alliances allegedly marked Trump’s Middle East policy in his first term, and set him on the road to an illegal andunwinnable war against Iranin his second. The central characters in that sordid set of machinations were his own son-in-law and senior adviser Jared Kushner, a few Gulf rulers, and Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu — all working towards a plan to redraw the political map of West Asia. Iran was the adversary to be contained, and it was on this that they converged: a plan to “blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal”. Billions of dollars were allegedly paid to Kushner in what may be the biggest scandal in recent history — one that best defines the link between money and Trump’s conduct of his Middle East policy, and which has pushed the entire region into an intractable conflict with global consequences. A recently published book, Princes and Thieves by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, provides startling details on how billions of dollars were allegedly transferred into accounts — managed by Kushner — by Gulf sheikhdoms, to implement a plan to break Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran and change the “political map of the Middle East”. The author supports his view of the transactions with details drawn from accounts hacked by a Western intelligence agency, though Kushner has called the allegations fabricated. According to the author, the transfers began in 2017 and were well underway by the spring of 2018, during Trump’s first term — when Kushner served as the president’s special envoy on the Middle East. While he had very close relations with Israel, he also cultivated strong business and diplomatic connections with willing Gulf sheikhdoms to allegedly pay for influence with the Trump administration. >A recent book details how money and corruption were leveraged to redesign the Middle East. According to the author, “Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ), and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept”. The convergence againstObama’s nuclear dealwith Iran — formally the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — brought Saudi Arabia and the UAE together on the issue. Agreed on July 14, 2015, between Iran and the P5+1, and endorsed by Security Council Resolution 2231, the deal came into effect in January 2016. Under it, Iran capped its enrichment at 3.67 per cent, cut its centrifuge numbers and opened its nuclear facilities to IAEA inspection. In return, nuclear-related sanctions on Iran were lifted on oil exports, banking, and SWIFT access, with frozen assets to be released in stages. But Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE had strong reservations. Each opposed the JCPOA for different reasons and with different intensity; the common ground was that the agreement was too narrow and too temporary, its restrictions written to expire under sunset clauses. Israel openly campaigned against it, and the two Gulf states lobbied against it too. For deal sceptics, Trump’s election in 2016 was good news. In May 2018, the president withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions in phases under a “maximum pressure” campaign. The move brought the Gulf nations closer to the Trump administration. The billions alleged to have flowed into Kushner’s accounts appeared to have delivered. The book maintains that early in Trump’s first term, “MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals”. Both Arab rulers saw this as part of an effort to help Trump win a second presidency. In the same period, Kushner conceived the so-called Abraham Accords aimed at normalisation between Israel and the Arab states. He owned the file. No State Department desk, no regional bureau, no ambassador in the chain: a son-in-law with a security clearance and a direct line to the president negotiated directly with the Gulf rulers, according to the book. One goal was to sideline the question of a separate Palestinian state. The UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan signed. The book also reveals that during that period Kushner helped negotiate a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE — the arrangement that later became public as the Abraham Accords. Cole writes that “Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE against a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of that emergency defence, and its government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defence fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia. “Although Kushner’s position as senior adviser to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosure for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House he had to file both a public and a confidential financial form, the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory — or beneficiary — access.” But apparently, the president’s son-in-law did not comply. The writer quotes a source that Kushner “promised MBZ he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalisation with Israel so that business could take off”. For the Gulf Arab governments, money was not a problem. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent,” the source told the author. The book exposes the sordid linkage between power and corruption that marked Trump’s presidency. It also lays bare the unholy alliance between Israel and the Gulf governments, formed to change the political map of the Middle East. In the end, this design has left the region more destabilised than before.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Hidden cause of economic imbalances
articles.content: GROWING inequality is a serious economic and social issue. Internally, we tend to treat poverty and inequality as separate problems. They are closely connected but not identical. Poverty is about deprivation; inequality is about how income, wealth, opportunities, and economic power are distributed. An economy can grow and even reduce poverty temporarily while allowing wealth and privilege to become concentrated. Household data underlines the problem. The consumption-based Gini coefficient increased from 28.4 in 2018 –19 to 32.7 in 2024 –25. This figure does not capture the full extent of inequality in income and wealth, because household surveys tend to underrepresent the assets and incomes of the richest households. The distribution of income and wealth influences what people consume, what businesses produce, where investment flows, and how much a country imports. In Pakistan, a relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets, while much of the population struggles to meet basic needs. A relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets. The benefits of economic growth have been distributed unevenly. Expanding sectors such as banking, telecommunications, IT, energy, oil and gas require capital, technology, and specialised skills, favouring those who already possess financial resources or access to quality education. The state’s failure to provide decent education and healthcare has denied much of the population a fair opportunity to participate in these activities. Hence, economic disadvantages are passed from one generation to the next. Equally damaging is the continued protection of selected businesses from competition through high import duties, subsidies, tax exemptions, and special regulatory concessions. Powerful business groups have resisted competition, sometimes forming cartels to influence prices and markets. Profits earned through state protection rather than efficiency reward influence instead of innovation, raise costs for consumers, and weaken competitiveness. The tax system has reinforced these inequalities by treating similar incomes from different sources unequally. Salaried individuals face substantial income taxes, while earnings from property, capital gains, and certain commercial activities have historically enjoyed relatively favourable treatment. The state itself has been a major contributor to wealth concentration. Valuable public land and plots have been given to officials and influential individuals, while discretionary powers over building permissions, zoning regulations, and public contracts have created opportunities for private enrichment. Rising property prices, reinforced by speculative investment and the use of real estate to park undeclared wealth, have further increased the fortunes of existing asset owners. Corruption, smuggling, tax evasion, and manipulation of import and export prices have provided additional avenues for accumulating wealth, often beyond the reach of effective taxation and accountability. Together, these factors constitute a system in which public authority is used to transfer economic opportunities and resources to privileged groups. The consequences extend beyond unfair income distribution; they also distort how the economy allocates and uses its scarce resources. When fortunes can be made through political connections, regulatory concessions, and protection from competition, capital and entrepreneurial talent are diverted towards securing favours rather than productive investment. It becomes more profitable to lobby for higher import duties or special exemptions than to invest in technology, improve quality, or develop export markets. The concentration of purchasing power also shapes the structure of domestic demand and, therefore, what businesses choose to produce. Businesses often respond to this purchasing power by directing investment towards activities serving a narrow market. Meanwhile, the limited purchasing power of the majority constrains demand for mass-consumption goods, discouraging investment in industries that could serve a broader domestic market, create jobs, and compete globally. This distorted pattern of consumption and production also contributes to our recurring external imbalances. The concentration of disposable income generates demand for imported vehicles, electronics, luxury goods, foreign travel, and education abroad, adding to the foreign exchange needed for machinery, fuel, technology, and industrial inputs. Not all imports are undesirable. Many are essential for productivity and exports. However, our consumption and production structures generate substantial demand for foreign exchange without a corresponding capacity to earn it through competitive exports. Remittancesfrom overseas Pakistanis have helped bridge this gap. But however valuable these inflows, they cannot substitute indefinitely for an economy capable of financing its import requirements through its own export earnings. Inequality is certainly not the sole cause of external deficits. Exchange rate policies, tariffs, energy costs, inflation, low productivity, and weak export competitiveness also matter. Still, the concentration of purchasing power helps explain why import demand remains substantial even when we face severe foreign exchange constraints. There is another damaging effect. When influential groups secure tax exemptions, subsidies, and protected markets, government revenues suffer. The burden of financing an oversized, extractive state, with its extensive controls and perks and privileges, consequently falls disproportionately on salaried workers, compliant businesses, and ordinary consumers unable to escape taxation. Public expenditure compounds the problem. Chronicunderinvestment in quality educationand healthcare has denied millions of children a fair start. Affluent households can purchase good private education and medical care, while poorer families depend on poor and overstretched public services. Their children’s prospects depend on family circumstances. The failure to provide equal opportunities thereby perpetuates inequality across generations. Addressing these disparities does not mean penalising wealth creation. It means distinguishing wealth earned through enterprise, innovation, and productivity from fortunes accumulated through political connections, monopolies, and state-granted privileges. This requires a fairer tax system. Protection must give way to competition, while discretionary allocations of public land, contracts, and regulatory concessions need to be replaced by transparent, rule-based processes. Foreign aid, remittances, and favourable global developments have provided only temporary relief, enabling successive governments to shelve tough reforms, thereby sustaining an economic structure that rewards privilege over productivity. Unless this system of privileges and unequal opportunities is dismantled, Pakistan will remain trapped in recurring internal and external imbalances, regardless of how many stabilisation programmes it negotiates with the IMF and others. The writer is a former governor of the State Bank.
articles.author: Shahid Kardar

articles.title: American dilemma
articles.content: “IRAN militarily is effectively over,” the US president declared on Monday following talks with the Qatari prime minister. “We’re just keeping it the status quo … at the behest” of Iran’s neighbours. The Gulf states include some of Donald Trump’s biggest benefactors, and they have borne the brunt of Iranian military retaliation. Trump has also acknowledged that the domestic unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran contributed to the comprehensive thrashing his Republican Party received in last week’s midterm elections, yet insisted he had no regrets because the goal of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remained paramount. That’s an absurd premise in a variety of ways; besides, Iran is unlikely to consider the conflict over as long as it is militarily menaced by a superpower or its regional proxies. What’s notable, though, is that unlike most US aggressions against faraway nations, the majority opinion opposed the assault on Iran from the outset. The co-belligerent’s bloodlust presumably put the kibosh on jingoistic impulses. In a CBS interview on Sunday, Trump admitted that one reason for the midterm drubbing was that “there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel”. There’s nothing ‘incredible’ about popular distaste for a genocidal power, especially when your tax dollars are enabling its egregious excesses. It’s true that anti-Israel sentiment paid dividends for candidates across large parts of the US, but the infamous American Israel Public Affairs Committee and other pro-Zionist PACS also scored many successes even as their biggest bets didn’t pay off. AIPAC’s chief bête noire was Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who in his victory speech thanked the committee, which contributed nearly $40 million to his opponents, for “giving me the opportunity to beat you twice” — in the primary and on election day. What will the Democrats do with their mandate? On election eve, Trump announced that nearly $4 billion in annual aid would no longer flow to Israel. That’s unlikely to have affected anyone’s voting intentions, given that presidential pronouncements are notoriously unreliable. But even if there is a halt, far larger avenues of military assistance will remain open, including clauses in the $1.5 trillion 2027 defence budget that effectively embed the Israel Defence Forces in the Pentagon. It’s hard to imagine any serious objections from the AIPAC-aligned Democratic leadership personified by Chuck Schumer in the Senate and Hakeem Jeffries in the House of Representatives. A growing number of incoming Democratic senators and representatives are keen to dispense with the services of this discredited duo. For the moment though, that’s just wishful thinking. But things could change. The realisation seems to have seeped in that unless the Democrats, with large majorities in both Houses of Congress, begin to deliver on campaign promises, there could be a backlash in 2028. The key issues are mostly domestic, from blatant corruption and the cost of living (exacerbated by the Iran conflict) to healthcare costs, unregulated AI, resource-hungry data centres, and the impunity of tech plutocrats. Elon Musk poured nearly $500m into the midterms, all in vain; he focused on Texas, which turned a bright blue. But the question is whether he can be held to account for his role as head of the now disbanded department of government efficiency, among other misdeeds. The anti-Trump Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has already introduced articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, hoping that Trump will fire him before the Democrats assume congressional power in January. Massie’s efforts won’t pay off, but will the Democrats do any better? Will they hold Stephen Miller to account for his dedication to deporting ‘illegal aliens’ by brutal means? Several of the Democrats freshly elected to national office — and many more at the state level — will strive to do their best by their constituents. All too many others, however, have yet to be disabused of the notion that gravitating to the centre is the safest option, even if no measurable progress is achieved. The New York Times editorialised at length on Monday about the wisdom of combining economic ‘populism’ with social conservatism. This is a blueprint for a bridge to nowhere. The Democrats ought to have realised this long ago, but perhaps it’s not too late. Miller took over as Trump’s chief of staff, indicating a doubling down on his worst impulses, just as the president rescinded his acceptance of last week’s results. It’s a pity that Trump’s invitation to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White to serve as his press secretary so that the “violent Fighter and Warrior” and his employees could “defend us against the Lunatic Left” turned out to be a joke. Fleetingly, I was reminded of how the Roman emperor Commodus ultimately encountered a wrestler.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Values in education
articles.content: SCHOOLS are entrusted with the responsibility of helping students develop their skills to meet the challenges ahead. Skills broadly refer to critical thinking, creativity, communication, and the like. Skills for the future are mostly geared towards developing higher-order thinking so students can become independent and lifelong learners, with curiosity to explore, ability to innovate, and willingness to bring about positive change. Within these parameters is a human side to education — where students’ propensity to respond to what they are taught is closely linked to their affinity with the environment. Studies show that students benefit from learning when they feel valued by their teachers and peers. Their willingness to contribute in class stems from positive interactions. Globally, as schools work on student and teacher well-being, this phenomenon has become embedded in the school culture. Schools operate as communities, an extension of family, where academic goals are intertwined with shared commitment to goals and values, where there is acceptance of different perspectives. The cue that children get in such an environment is: ‘I matter’. Children with a deep sense of belonging at school know that they will be protected against discrimination and disorder. They know they can speak up in class without being scoffed at, and they are encouraged to demonstrate a sense of purpose and agency. What is the role of teachers in fostering such an environment? Teachers have long been role models for students. Their words and actions have ripple effects that percolate far down the corridors — from classrooms to common rooms, from the staff rooms to the playground and beyond. Students imbibe communication skills, confidence, rules of engagement, and personal values from their teachers. They watch and learn throughout their school lives. Teachers become carriers of school culture and values. This also means microaggressions can become normalised very quickly. If, for example, a teacher brushes off a student’s comments or reacts angrily to them, the response becomes acceptable to the students, who will demonstrate similar behaviour amongst themselves. Students benefit from learning when they feel valued. The human side of education implies looking closely at what the students are learning. What behavioural standards have they come to accept as their own? What expectations do their teachers have of them? Students pick up signals from their environment very early on. Holistic education is not confined to a robust curriculum. It includes values inculcated in classrooms, the mindset and behaviour that define the culture of an educational institution. Schools that have built and sustained a positive culture where students feel valued have done so over time with structured strategies. Unacceptable social behaviour or incidental infractions are not left unaddressed, nor are there harsh consequences. In fact, research shows that harsh consequences in which students are berated, ostracised, or subjected to humiliation will harden them to the point where they progressively defy authority. The big challenge for students in such environments is not to avoid breaking rules or defying expectations but to perfect the strategies to avoid being caught. The more time a student spends avoiding consequences, the more it affects their overall motivation and ability to focus on academic goals. School life becomes more about avoiding getting into trouble than about doing better in their studies. School culture and its embedded values are important for this very reason — so students can spend time on actually working on meeting curriculum standards and involving themselves in healthy co-curricular and community activities. Students need to spend time embodying the role of responsible citizenship. Many of these values are developed in their foundational years and beyond, mainly through early intervention. Early intervention can take the form of social-emotional learning that is embedded in the curriculum framework throughout the school years. Students are taught emotional regulation in their interactions, and self-expression and agency in social engagement. Individual strengths are celebrated, personal stories shared, and opportunities created for students’ voices to be heard in small groups and larger forums. When teachers celebrate positive behaviour in public and with parents, students begin to recognise and follow expectations. Some schools provide practical techniques for behaviour reinforcement at home. Many schools organise learning workshops with the senior students so the mantle is carried forward — ‘this is how we do things around here’ is the legacy students imbibe from their seniors and their teachers. The writer is a teacher educator, author and Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, UK.
articles.author: Neda Mulji

articles.title: Opposition moves
articles.content: THE opposition alliance TTAP hashinted at another anti-government drive. Its recent talks with the JUI-F on parliamentary coordination indicate that the party’s chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman is poised to lead the campaign. All this raises obvious questions: is the opposition seriously planning an anti-government drive? Is it actually convinced that such a movement at this time can remove the government? Will the pragmatic JUI-F chief join such an effort? At least for now, the answer may disappoint the opposition’s supporters. The PTI is locked in a protracted battle with the government, while much of its top leadership remains behind bars. It has twice attempted to mobilise public support for a mass movement and rally people around its political objectives since the controversial February 2024 elections, but both attempts failed. It is obvious that people, particularly in Punjab and Sindh, are not ready to join any such movement at this time. Even in KP, where the PTI had been in power since 2013, the party has failed to mobilise the public. TheJamaat-i-Islami’s driveagainst high petrol prices similarly failed to bring people out onto the streets. Though the JUI-F has staunch supporters on the streets who are ready to answer their party’s call, its leader has never been one to take needless risks. His azadi march against the PTI government brought thousands of supporters to Islamabad, but failed to dislodge the Imran Khan administration. The sit-in was eventually called off without achieving its objective. The federal government has imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP, claiming they were necessary for security and administrative reasons. The opposition sees these moves as an assault on provincial autonomy. Maulana Fazlur Rahman is actively opposing the move. The government’s response to his criticism has fuelled fears that the JUI-F could face the same crackdown as the PTI. Those concerns are not difficult to understand. The recent actions of the Balochistan government against JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza on a questionable citizenship claim reinforce these fears. Yet expectations of the maulana leading another street confrontation with the government anytime soon are likely to remain wishful thinking. Nevertheless, this consensus of politicians of different persuasions reflects a growing frustration with the government’s high-handed actions. Thelawyers’ emergencein this arena is particularly significant. The All Pakistan Lawyers Action Committee in Quetta has vowed to support Senator Murtaza and resist any attempt to undermine constitutional supremacy. There are also reports of raids on lawyers’ homes. Although the prospects of a new anti-government movement remain remote, public discontent should not be ignored. Small, isolated protests and expressions of dissent can gradually gather momentum and develop into a much larger movement.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: CT battle
articles.content: IN order to stem the tide of terrorism, it is necessary to ensure that no spaces are left for violent elements to operate in the country. Terrorists often try to blend in with the civilian population. Intelligence-based operations are meant to counter this practice. The military has recentlysaidthat two mosques being misused by TTP terrorists in North Waziristan have been cleared. As per ISPR, the terrorists had desecrated the places of worship to store explosives, while also operating torture cells inside the mosques. In the twisted worldview of the TTP and those of their ilk, misusing mosques — as well as attacking the faithful inside places of worship — is acceptable, hence these developments do not come as a surprise. What is important is for operations against violent anti-state elements to continue so that these groups are rooted out for good. It does seem that the state’s efforts are bearing fruit. According to figuresreleasedrecently by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, terrorist attacks in October fell by 37pc as compared to September. Improvements were particularly seen in Balochistan and KP — the provinces hardest hit by various strands of terrorism. Yet in KP’s merged districts, where the problem of terrorism is most acute, the gains were modest: October saw 30 attacks compared to 34 in September. Action against terrorist groups must continue until all areas are declared clear of militancy. While the Taliban are reluctant to cooperate against terrorists who launch attacks on Pakistan from Afghan soil, the state here must do all possible to ensure violent elements have no safe spaces within our borders. The gains made over the last month should be capitalised on, with the affected areas permanently cleared of terrorists. These counterterrorism operations must come with minimal displacement of the local people. For over two decades, tribal communities and those living in disturbed areas have faced repeated terrorist violence and displacement due to CT operations. This time the state should ensure that after the terrorism-hit areas are cleared, the government builds on the gains so that local people can live in peace. More IBOs and securing the border against terrorist infiltrators can help bring long-term peace.
articles.author: Editorial
